title: You are the man (2 Samuel 12:1–13)
hook: Nathan tells a story about a poor man's lamb, and David convicts himself
carry: I have sinned against the Lord

segments.voice: Yesterday, Uriah, the loyal soldier, and a king who used his power to take and to kill. Your line was power can rot.

Uriah is dead. Bathsheba lives in David's house. A son is born. The text records no one saying a word to the king. Then the prophet Nathan comes, sent by God. He doesn't accuse anyone. He asks the king for a ruling on a case. Two men in one city, he says, one rich and one poor. The rich man had flocks and herds, a great many. The poor man had nothing but one little ewe lamb. And David, who was a shepherd before he was a king, leans in to listen.
screen: `A SON IS BORN. NO ONE SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Nathan describes that lamb, in the King James Bible: it "grew up together with him, and with his children; it did eat of his own meat, and drank of his own cup, and lay in his bosom, and was unto him as a daughter." A pet. Family. Then a traveler visits the rich man, who doesn't want to take from his own flock, so he takes the poor man's lamb and serves it for dinner. David explodes: "As the LORD liveth, the man that hath done this thing shall surely die." The lamb must be repaid fourfold, because the man had no pity. He has pronounced the sentence. And Nathan says it: "Thou art the man." The story was a mirror, and David walked right up to it. Nathan goes on in God's name: I anointed you, I gave you everything, and if that had been too little I would have given you more. Why did you despise the commandment? You killed Uriah with the sword of the Ammonites, and took his wife. A king could have had him thrown out. David doesn't. He says: "I have sinned against the LORD." No excuse. No list of reasons. Nathan answers at once: "The LORD also hath put away thy sin; thou shalt not die." Forgiven, though the chapter goes on to say there will still be consequences. The heading of Psalm fifty-one ties that psalm to this very moment, when Nathan came to David, and some Christians pray it as a prayer of repentance.

Think of the last time someone told you something true about yourself that you didn't want to hear, and go back to it slowly with one question: was any of it true? If some of it was, don't defend yourself in your head; just let it stand there, like Nathan in the doorway. If you pray, you can bring it before God in silence.
Nathan. The prophet who told David a story about a rich man and a poor man's lamb, until the king realized he was the guilty judge.
Your line: I have sinned against the Lord. Six words, said without a single excuse. That's day seven hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Some Christians read Nathan's rebuke together with Psalm 51, whose heading links it to this moment, and some pray Psalm 51 as a prayer of confession.

original.note: Hebrew: you are the man, Nathan's words to David (2 Samuel 12:7).

trapdoor: what you thought: a phrase for praising someone: you're the man.
what it means: Nathan's verdict on David, after David condemned the rich man in Nathan's story.
what a scholar hears: attah ha-ish; the king judged the case, and the case was himself.

chat.says: How did Nathan get King David to admit what he'd done?
options: He told a story about a stolen lamb, then said: thou art the man.
He gathered the army and threatened to remove David from the throne.
He showed the king Uriah's letter, so David couldn't deny it.
chat.meaning: Nathan's story let David pass sentence on the rich man; then Nathan said, Thou art the man, and David confessed.

Ammonites.meaning: an enemy people Israel's army was fighting

Psalm fifty-one.meaning: a psalm of repentance, tied by its heading to this moment

notes: Consequences (12:10–14, including the death of the child) are summarized as 'there will still be consequences'; Keeper to decide whether to name more.
The carry 'you are the man' modernizes the KJV 'Thou art the man'.
David as a former shepherd is from 1 Samuel 16–17 (earlier days).
